summary.text: Lottery mathematics calculates the probabilities of winning or losing a lottery game.
It is based mainly on combinatorics, in particular combinations without replacement.
To be sure of a jackpot in a 6/49 game you would need 13,983,816 different tickets, one for every possible number combination.

facts.label: Jackpot cover
facts.value: 13,983,816 tickets cover every combination in a 6/49 game

facts.label: Only sure way
facts.value: Buy a ticket for every possible number combination

facts.label: Small guarantee
facts.value: In 5-from-90 lotto, 100 tickets guarantee a ticket with two matches

facts.label: Repeat draw
facts.value: In Bulgaria's 6/49 lottery, the same six numbers came up twice in four days

facts.label: Also useful for
facts.value: Analysing coincidences, like repeated numbers across draws

items.prompt: A friend says that picking numbers from family birthdays guarantees a jackpot. What is the only way to be certain of winning?

options.label: Buy a ticket for every possible number combination
Pick numbers that have not been drawn recently
Choose numbers spread evenly over the whole range
Play the same ticket in every single draw

items.explain: There is only one way to ensure a jackpot: buy at least one ticket for every possible combination.

items.prompt: A syndicate buys every ticket to guarantee the jackpot, but it is likely that several other winners will share it. How should the winnings be counted?

options.label: Count the full jackpot as if the syndicate won it alone
Count only the syndicate's likely share of the jackpot
Ignore the jackpot and count only the smaller prizes
Count the jackpot twice, once for each ticket

items.explain: If the jackpot will probably be split, only your likely share counts towards the total the tickets win.

items.prompt: In a lottery draw, a ball that has been pulled out is set aside and cannot come out again. What is this way of drawing called?

options.label: Drawing with replacement
Drawing in random order
Drawing without replacement
Drawing from a sample

items.explain: The winning balls are drawn from the pool without replacement, which is why the maths uses combinations without replacement.

items.prompt: The same six numbers came up in two draws in a row. What does lottery mathematics offer here?

options.label: Proof that the second draw was influenced by the first
A tool to analyse how unusual such a coincidence really is
A rule that repeated numbers can never be calculated
A reason to avoid numbers that were drawn before

items.explain: Such repeats look implausible for random outcomes, and lottery mathematics can be used to analyse these extraordinary events.

items.prompt: Someone wants the smallest number of tickets that guarantees at least two matching numbers. How easy is it to work out?

options.label: Easy, with the same formula as the jackpot case
Easy, because it is just half of all combinations
Impossible, because lotteries are random
Hard, and often an open problem

items.explain: Finding the minimum number of tickets that guarantees at least 2 matches is a hard and often open problem.

items.prompt: A lottery uses a drum of 49 balls and each ticket lists 6 numbers. In the standard formulas, which letter stands for the 49?

options.label: T, the numbers on a ticket
P, the balls in the pool
M, the numbers that match
W, the balls that are drawn

items.explain: P is the number of balls in the pool, T is the number on a ticket, M the matches and W the winning balls drawn.
